comparison: Both evaluate NOLC1 upregulation in GC (C28, C35-C38). OpenEval finds evidence SUPPORTED by multiple methods (IHC, WB, TCGA). Peer reviewers also accept this finding as part of study strengths, with editor noting 'evidence supporting conclusions is solid.'

Both address survival correlations (C39-C41). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED by Kaplan-Meier analysis from public databases. Peer reviewers accept without challenge, with one noting 'significant correlation between high NOLC1 expression and poor prognosis.'

Both evaluate NOLC1 in cisplatin-resistant cells (C42-C44). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED by WB and IF with validated resistance markers. Peer reviewers accept this as study foundation, acknowledging 'upregulation of NOLC1 was associated with cis-resistant GC.'

Both assess NOLC1 knockdown effects on cisplatin sensitivity (C45-C49). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED by multiple assays (CCK-8, colony formation, apoptosis). Peer reviewers accept, summarizing 'knocking down NOLC1 increased GC sensitivity to Cis.' OpenEval also covers DNA damage (C50) which peer review acknowledges indirectly.

OpenEval evaluates DNA damage evidence (C50) as SUPPORTED by comet assay and γ-H2AX staining. Peer review R4 implicitly accepts this as part of the sensitization mechanism but does not specifically discuss DNA damage markers.

Both evaluate in vivo xenograft validation (C51-C54). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED by tumor volume, H&E, and IHC with adequate sample sizes. Peer reviewers accept without challenge, with editor stating 'evidence supporting conclusions is solid.'

Both address ferroptosis morphology and pharmacological validation (C55-C60). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED by TEM and rescue experiments with erastin/Fer-1. Peer reviewers express UNCERTAINTY, stating 'experiments to verify regulation of ferroptosis sensitivity by NOLC1 are sort of superficial' and requesting additional FIN validation.

Both evaluate ferroptosis markers LDH and mitochondrial membrane potential (C61-C63). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED by established assays. Peer reviewers express UNCERTAINTY as part of broader concern that 'more evidence supporting regulation of ferroptosis induced by Cisplatin by NOLC1 should be added.'

Both assess ROS measurements (C64-C66). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED by multiple complementary methods (DCFH-DA, MitoPeDPP, H2O2 assay). Peer reviewers express UNCERTAINTY, requesting more robust ferroptosis evidence as part of editor's call for 'new experiments regarding ferroptosis-associated studies.'

Both evaluate ferroptosis regulatory proteins (C67-C70). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED by WB and IHC showing GPX4↓, FSP1↓, ACSL4↑. Peer reviewers express UNCERTAINTY, concerned that ferroptosis verification is insufficient and requesting validation with additional ferroptosis inducers.

Both address p53 protein levels and transcriptional activity (C71-C73). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED, noting the paradoxical decrease in protein despite increased transcription. Peer reviewers accept this as key finding, with editor confirming 'novel role of NOLC1 in regulating p53 nuclear transcriptional activity.'

Both evaluate p53 transcriptional activity (C74-C77). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED by dual-luciferase assays and RT-qPCR of target genes. Peer reviewers accept, stating 'NOLC1 could bind to p53 and decrease its nuclear transcriptional activity,' treating transcriptional data as well-supported.

Both address NOLC1-p53 binding prediction (C78-C80). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED by molecular docking but notes need for experimental validation. Peer reviewers accept the interaction data, though one raises concern about 'excessive contrast adjustment' in Western blot images (Figure 5G/5I).

Both evaluate experimental validation of NOLC1-p53 interaction (C81-C82). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED by Co-IP and IF. Peer reviewers accept, stating 'NOLC1 could bind to p53,' though technical image quality concerns are noted for related figures.

Both assess p53 nuclear localization (C83-C85). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED by IF with quantification and nuclear/cytoplasmic fractionation. Peer reviewers accept this mechanism, confirming 'novel role of NOLC1 in regulating p53 nuclear transcriptional activity.'

Both evaluate domain mapping of NOLC1-p53 interaction (C86-C87). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED by Co-IP with domain constructs validating DBD binding. Peer reviewers accept the interaction data as demonstrated, treating it as part of the established mechanism.

Both address p53 DNA binding inhibition (C88). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED by ChIP-seq but suggests additional validation. Peer reviewers accept this as part of the mechanism showing NOLC1 'decrease its nuclear transcriptional activity,' treating DNA binding data as well-supported.

Both evaluate the dual mechanism conclusion (C89-C90). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED by convergence of multiple experiments. Peer reviewers accept, confirming the 'novel role of NOLC1 in regulating p53 nuclear transcriptional activity' encompasses both cytoplasmic retention and DNA binding inhibition.

Both address MDM2 expression changes (C91-C92). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED by RT-qPCR, noting C92 is appropriately labeled as speculation. Peer reviewers accept this as part of p53 regulation mechanism without specific challenge to the MDM2 data.

Both evaluate p53-MDM2 feedback loop background (C93-C95). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED by established literature (Brooks and Gu, 2006). Peer reviewers implicitly accept this well-established knowledge as appropriate background for investigating p53 degradation.

Both assess MDM2 regulation by NOLC1 (C96-C97). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED by RT-qPCR, WB, and IHC. Peer reviewers accept this as part of the p53-MDM2 feedback loop mechanism without raising specific concerns about the MDM2 data.

Both evaluate p53 stability and ubiquitination (C98-C101). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED by turnover and ubiquitination assays. Peer reviewers accept the mechanism but note 'role of MDM2/p53 in ferroptosis or cisplatin resistance mediated by NOLC1 should be further studied,' indicating acceptance but requesting deeper validation.

Both address p53 rescue experiments for cisplatin sensitivity (C102-C103). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED by p53 siRNA rescue but suggests additional validation. Peer reviewers express UNCERTAINTY, stating rescue experiments are 'acknowledged but considered insufficient,' requesting 'genetic manipulation of p53' for robust confirmation.

Both evaluate p53 rescue at ferroptosis marker level (C104-C105). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED by WB of ferroptosis markers after p53 knockdown. Peer reviewers express UNCERTAINTY, considering this 'key evidence to confirm contribution to NOLC1 regulation' but insufficient without more comprehensive genetic manipulation.

Both assess immunogenic cell death markers (C106-C110). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED by LDH, HMGB1, and CRT measurements. Peer reviewers express UNCERTAINTY, noting concerns about ferroptosis evidence extend to ICD conclusions since 'they depend on establishing ferroptosis as the mechanism.'

Both evaluate in vivo immunotherapy combination (C111-C114). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED by MFC model data with appropriate controls. Peer reviewers express UNCERTAINTY, acknowledging therapeutic benefit but stating 'mechanistic link to ferroptosis requires stronger validation' per editor's call for more robust ferroptosis studies.

Both assess histological validation in vivo (C115-C116). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED by H&E and IHC of multiple markers. Peer reviewers express UNCERTAINTY about underlying mechanism, though histological data are acknowledged as part of observed therapeutic benefit.

Both evaluate in vivo p53 nuclear localization (C117-C118). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED by IHC validating in vitro mechanism. Peer reviewers express UNCERTAINTY, acknowledging the observation but concerned about the ferroptosis mechanistic link requiring stronger validation.

Both address in vivo ferroptosis markers (C119-C122). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED by Liperfluo staining and serum HMGB1. Peer reviewers express UNCERTAINTY, noting editor's requirement for 'more robust conclusions regarding ferroptosis-associated studies' applies to these in vivo findings.

Both evaluate CTL infiltration (C123-C126). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED by FACS with validated gating strategy and IF. Peer reviewers accept as SUPPORTED, acknowledging 'potential role of NOLC1 in targeted therapy for GC' and treating immune profiling as well-demonstrated.

Both assess cytokine profiles (C127-C130). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED by ELISA showing anti-tumor immune response. Peer reviewers accept as SUPPORTED, treating immune profiling data combined with CTL infiltration as well-supported evidence for enhanced immunotherapy response.

Both evaluate treatment safety (C131-C133). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED by biochemical analysis and organ H&E, though notes limitations of low dose/short duration. Peer reviewers accept without challenge, not disputing the 'no side effects' claim for the preclinical setting.
